# EBS and instance store: say it

<!-- speak:start id=ebs-s01 -->
### Prompt 1

**A customer asks.** If that instance fails tomorrow, what do we lose, and how long are we offline?

<details>
<summary>Answer</summary>

**In 10 seconds.** If the instance fails, the volume survives and we attach it again. If the zone fails, we restore last night's snapshot within hours.

**In 60 seconds.**

The short answer is: if only the instance fails, we lose nothing on the database disk.

It works like this. The database writes to a volume, a disk that lives apart from the instance.

AWS copies the volume inside its zone, against hardware faults.

If the instance dies, we attach the volume to a new instance in that zone.

Every night, we also take a snapshot: a copy kept across the whole Region.

If the volume or its zone fails, we rebuild it from that snapshot in another zone.

The thing to watch is this. AWS doesn't back up volumes, so we automate the snapshots.

A rebuild takes hours, and the new volume is slow at first.

In your case, a zone failure costs at most one day of new data.

Can our customers accept losing one day of analysis in the worst case?

**Skeleton.** instance fails: volume survives / copied inside one zone / nightly snapshot, rebuild anywhere / snapshots are our job

**Must say.**

- An EBS volume is off-instance storage that persists independently of its instance; a new instance must be in the same Availability Zone to attach it.
- A volume is automatically replicated within its Availability Zone, which protects against the failure of a single hardware component.
- AWS does not automatically back up the volume data; regular snapshots are the customer's job, and Data Lifecycle Manager or AWS Backup can automate them.
- Snapshot data is replicated across all Availability Zones of the Region, so you can restore the volume in any zone of that Region.

**Do not say.**

- "AWS backs up the disk for us.". Say: AWS does not automatically back up EBS volume data. Snapshots are our job, so we automate them.
- "We lose nothing, ever.". Say: Replication inside the zone covers a single hardware failure. After a zone failure we restore the newest snapshot, so newer data is lost.
- "The restored disk is fast at once.". Say: A volume restored from a snapshot shows increased I/O latency until its blocks are downloaded from Amazon S3.

**Follow-up questions.**

- What if someone deletes the volume by mistake? The newest snapshot alone can rebuild the volume. Recycle Bin can also restore deleted EBS volumes and snapshots for a time period that you specify, if a retention rule exists.
- What happens to the volumes if we terminate the instance? By default, the root volume is deleted when the instance terminates, and other EBS volumes are kept. The DeleteOnTermination attribute of each volume changes this.

</details>
<!-- speak:end -->

<!-- speak:start id=ebs-s02 -->
### Prompt 2

**A customer asks.** The AWS page says io2 is for databases. Should we pay for io2, or is gp3 enough for our Postgres?

<details>
<summary>Answer</summary>

**In 10 seconds.** Start on gp3. It fits medium-sized databases at a lower cost. Move to io2 Block Express when your latency or IOPS needs outgrow gp3.

**In 60 seconds.**

Both gp3 and io2 are SSD volumes that can run your Postgres database.

The difference is latency, durability and price.

It works like this. With gp3, you buy IOPS and throughput without buying more space.

Every gp3 volume starts at three thousand IOPS. You add more, up to five hundred IOPS per gibibyte.

io2 Block Express adds sub-millisecond latency and higher durability, for a higher price.

AWS suggests io2 when you need more than gp3 can give.

The thing to watch is the instance. Its own EBS limit can cap any volume.

So a faster volume can change nothing if the instance is the bottleneck.

In your case, I'd start on gp3 and watch the latency and IOPS metrics.

What latency and how many IOPS does your database need at the peak today?

**Skeleton.** both SSD, both run databases / gp3: buy IOPS without space / io2: lower latency, higher durability / instance can cap the volume

**Must say.**

- gp3 suits applications that need a balance between cost and performance, including medium-sized single-instance databases.
- With gp3 you provision IOPS and throughput independently of volume size, within a ratio of 500 IOPS per GiB, and every gp3 volume includes 3,000 IOPS.
- AWS recommends io2 Block Express for higher durability, better latency consistency, or more IOPS and throughput than gp3 can provide.
- io2 Block Express is designed for 99.999 percent volume durability, and gp3 for 99.8 percent to 99.9 percent.

**Do not say.**

- "Every production database needs io2.". Say: gp3 fits medium-sized single-instance databases. AWS recommends io2 Block Express when the needs go beyond what gp3 can provide.
- "gp3 is only for test systems.". Say: gp3 suits a balance between cost and performance, including medium-sized single-instance databases and boot volumes.
- "With io2 you don't need backups.". Say: Higher durability is not a backup. AWS does not automatically back up EBS volume data, so you still take snapshots.

**Follow-up questions.**

- How far can gp3 go before we have to switch? The maximum IOPS of one gp3 volume is 80,000. io2 Block Express reaches up to 256,000 IOPS on a Nitro-based instance.
- If we start on gp3, can we move to io2 later without downtime? Yes, on an instance that supports Elastic Volumes. You can change the volume type without detaching the volume or restarting the instance.

</details>
<!-- speak:end -->

### Prompt 3

**A customer asks.** Can all our web servers share one EBS volume with Multi-Attach, instead of paying for a file system?

<details>
<summary>Answer</summary>

**In 10 seconds.** No. Use Amazon EFS for shared files. Multi-Attach is for cluster software on io1 or io2 volumes in one Availability Zone.

**In 60 seconds.**

Both let several instances reach the same data, but in very different ways.

The short answer is no: for shared web files, use Amazon EFS.

It works like this. Multi-Attach gives one io2 volume to up to sixteen instances.

They must be Nitro instances in the same Availability Zone.

Every instance can write, so your software must keep writes from clashing.

Amazon EFS is a file system that instances in many zones mount together.

The thing to watch is the file system.

Normal ones like XFS aren't built for shared writes, so you need a clustered file system.

In your case, web files that every instance reads belong on Amazon EFS.

Do your web instances run in more than one Availability Zone?

**Skeleton.** both share data, differently / Multi-Attach: io2, one zone / software must coordinate writes / EFS: shared across zones

**Must say.**

- Multi-Attach attaches a single Provisioned IOPS SSD volume, io1 or io2, to several instances in the same Availability Zone.
- One Multi-Attach volume attaches to up to 16 instances built on the Nitro System.
- Standard file systems such as XFS and EXT4 are not designed for simultaneous access, so you use a clustered file system or an application that coordinates writes.
- Amazon EFS stores data within and across multiple Availability Zones and gives shared access to many EC2 instances.

**Do not say.**

- "Multi-Attach works across Availability Zones.". Say: Multi-Attach attaches one volume to instances in the same Availability Zone.
- "Any file system is safe on a Multi-Attach volume.". Say: Standard file systems such as XFS and EXT4 are not designed for simultaneous access. Use a clustered file system.
- "gp3 supports Multi-Attach.". Say: Multi-Attach is supported only on Provisioned IOPS SSD io1 and io2 volumes.

**Follow-up questions.**

- So when is Multi-Attach the right choice? When every instance is in one Availability Zone and the application is built on Windows Server Failover Cluster, uses NVMe reservations, or coordinates safe access at the application level.
- Why not put the shared files in Amazon S3 instead? Amazon S3 is an object storage service, and Amazon EFS is a file storage service. If your code reads and writes files by path, a file system is the closer fit.

</details>
<!-- speak:end -->

### Prompt 4

**A customer asks.** Our auditor found unencrypted volumes from last year. How do we encrypt them, and how do we stop this from happening again?

<details>
<summary>Answer</summary>

**In 10 seconds.** You can't encrypt them in place. Snapshot each one, restore it as an encrypted volume, and swap. Then turn on encryption by default.

**In 60 seconds.**

The short answer is: you can't switch on encryption for an existing volume.

You move the data to a new, encrypted volume, and you turn on encryption by default.

It works like this. You take a snapshot of the old volume.

From that snapshot, you create a new volume with encryption turned on.

In a short window, you stop the application, swap the volumes and start again.

Every snapshot of an encrypted volume is encrypted too.

The thing to watch is the default setting. It's per Region, and it doesn't touch old volumes.

So you turn it on in every Region you use.

Encryption keeps the same IOPS, with a minimal effect on latency.

In your case, turn on the default first, then replace the old volumes.

Which Regions does your team create volumes in?

**Skeleton.** no in-place encryption / snapshot, encrypted volume, swap / default is per Region / old volumes stay unencrypted

**Must say.**

- You cannot directly encrypt an existing unencrypted volume; you snapshot it and create a new encrypted volume from the snapshot.
- Encryption by default is a Region-specific setting, so you turn it on in each Region you use.
- Encryption by default has no effect on existing EBS volumes or snapshots.
- Snapshots of encrypted volumes, and volumes created from encrypted snapshots, are encrypted automatically.

**Do not say.**

- "Turning on encryption by default fixes the old volumes.". Say: Encryption by default has no effect on existing EBS volumes or snapshots. Old volumes need a snapshot and a new encrypted volume.
- "Encryption slows the database down.". Say: Encrypted volumes deliver the same IOPS as unencrypted volumes, with a minimal effect on latency.
- "We can encrypt the volume in place with Elastic Volumes.". Say: You cannot directly encrypt an existing unencrypted volume. Create a new encrypted volume from a snapshot of it.

**Follow-up questions.**

- Which key does encryption by default use? The AWS managed key aws/ebs, unless you choose a symmetric customer managed key. Choose a customer managed key if you plan to share snapshots with other accounts.
- After we turn it on, can someone opt out for one new volume in that Region? No, not for one volume. Once encryption by default is on in a Region, you cannot disable it for individual volumes or snapshots in that Region. It is a setting per Region, so check it in every Region that you use.

</details>
<!-- speak:end -->
